reference.source: Stiehm's Immune Deficiencies / Middleton's Allergy: Principles and Practice
clinicalPearls: One of the most common inherited immune variants, with low functional mannose-binding lectin found in a substantial minority of healthy people
Usually clinically silent and best regarded as a susceptibility modifier rather than a stand-alone immunodeficiency
Any predisposition is most relevant in early childhood before adaptive immunity matures, or when combined with another immune defect or immunosuppression
Reported associations include increased frequency or severity of pyogenic and respiratory infections and worse outcomes in some inflammatory or septic states
Low levels arise from common polymorphisms in the MBL2 structural gene and its promoter region
Diagnosis requires demonstrating low MBL level or impaired lectin pathway function, and low levels alone do not establish causation for a given infection
Management is supportive and directed at any co-existing immune defect, since no specific MBL replacement is in routine clinical use
reference.pathophysiology: Mannose-binding lectin is a circulating pattern-recognition molecule of the innate immune system that binds carbohydrate arrays on microbial surfaces and activates the lectin pathway of complement through MBL-associated serine proteases, promoting opsonisation and complement deposition independently of antibody. Common polymorphisms in the MBL2 gene reduce the amount of functional, correctly oligomerised protein, lowering lectin-pathway activity. Because this pathway provides an antibody-independent first line of defence, deficiency may leave a window of increased vulnerability, particularly in infancy or when other arms of immunity are compromised; however, redundancy with the classical and alternative complement pathways and with adaptive immunity means most deficient individuals remain healthy.
additionalDifferentials: Antibody deficiency syndromes (e.g. IgG subclass or specific antibody deficiency)
Ficolin or MASP2 lectin-pathway component deficiencies
Normal host with recurrent common childhood infections
additionalInvestigations: MBL2 genotyping for structural and promoter variants
Broader immune workup (immunoglobulins, specific antibodies, complement) to exclude co-existing defects
MASP2 and ficolin assessment where available if lectin-pathway defect suspected
Clinical correlation of infection history rather than reliance on the level alone
redFlags: Severe, recurrent or unusually invasive infection out of proportion to a minor MBL variant, prompting search for another immune defect
Deteriorating course of sepsis in a critically ill or immunosuppressed patient
Recurrent infection in an infant that persists beyond expected immune maturation
Concurrent features suggesting a more significant primary immunodeficiency
reference.prognosis: The great majority of individuals with low mannose-binding lectin are healthy and have a normal outlook; any excess infection risk is modest and mainly emerges in combination with immune immaturity, another immune defect, or immunosuppression.
pitfalls: Over-attributing a patient's recurrent infections to MBL deficiency and stopping the workup prematurely
Treating a common benign polymorphism as a serious primary immunodeficiency
Failing to look for a co-existing, more clinically important immune defect
Interpreting a single low MBL level without a functional lectin pathway assessment
management: Reassure that low mannose-binding lectin is usually clinically silent and is a susceptibility modifier rather than a stand-alone immunodeficiency
Treat intercurrent infections promptly with appropriate antimicrobials, as no routine replacement therapy is indicated
Ensure full immunisation, including pneumococcal and other polysaccharide-conjugate vaccines
Investigate for and manage any co-existing immune defect when infections are recurrent or unusually severe
Maintain heightened vigilance during infancy, chemotherapy or other immunosuppression when redundancy of immune defences is reduced
Involve clinical immunology and correlate the infection history with the deficiency rather than attributing causation to a low level alone
